Technical Steeps, Rock Rolls and Front-Brake Confidence

Performance outcome

The rider understands how steepness, surface, runout and traction change braking and body position on steeps and rock rolls, can describe the choices involved, and knows when to decline, walk or ask a coach.

Who it’s for

Advanced riders and racers preparing for steep, technical terrain, working with a coach.

Before this lesson

  • Advanced Body Position.
  • Brake to Go Faster.
  • A coach to select terrain and lead practice.

Why it matters

Steep, technical sections are where control matters most and where the consequences of losing it are highest. Understanding why braking and position change here makes coach-led practice far more productive.

Technical model

Reading the steep

Before riding, the questions are: how steep, what surface, where is the grip, where does it flatten out (the runout), and what happens if the rider has to stop? These decide whether and how a section should be ridden.

Front brake in context

One coaching view argues that many riders over-rely on the rear brake on steep ground and under-use the front, which, used with control and the right body position, can give more stopping power. This is one perspective: it is not a universal rule or a brake ratio, and the coach decides how it applies.

Body position on steep ground

Steep terrain tilts the bike, but gravity still pulls straight down. Riders need to keep their mass balanced over the bike, which usually means moving back relative to the bike while staying mobile, not locking out behind the saddle.

Declining is a skill

Choosing to walk a section, or to come back with a coach, is part of riding steep terrain well.

Physics & maths

Forces on a slope

On a slope of angle θ, gravity’s component along the slope is g sin θ, so the steeper the slope, the more braking force is needed just to hold a speed. Braking also shifts load onto the front wheel, which is why the front tyre has more grip available on steep ground, and why the rear tyre locks easily.

A good Mathlete visual: a slope-angle slider showing the along-slope component of gravity and the load split between the wheels.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Rear wheel locked and skidding down the steep.Over-reliance on the rear brake; braking where grip is lowest.Coach to supply
Locked out behind the saddle with straight arms.Fear; an outdated “weight right back” cue; no range left to absorb.Coach to supply
Committing without checking the runout.Not inspecting; social pressure.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
COACH-LED ONLY. The coach selects the venue, starting with lower-consequence terrain; this lesson does not recommend terrain.
Focus
Set by the coach.
Feedback
Coach observation and video review.

Stop when

  • Any loss of control.
  • Conditions change.
  • The rider wants to stop, or the coach calls it.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Inspection: does the rider check the steep and the runout first?
  • Brake control: is there skidding?
  • Position: mobile and balanced, or locked out?
  • Does the rider decline when appropriate?

Ready to move on

  • Set by the coach in person. Watching this lesson does not mean a rider is ready for steep terrain.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 3: high-consequence skills. Theory and expert references only. Any practical progression is authored and supervised in person by a verified specialist coach, in a suitable facility.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
